title: A distinctly disorganised dwarf
caption: The irregular dwarf galaxy UGC 4459, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: UGC 4459 · constellation Ursa Major · about 11 million light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: The diffuse, disorganised cloud of stars in this Hubble image is UGC 4459, an irregular dwarf galaxy about 11 million light-years away in Ursa Major. It has no clear structure: no central bulge of tightly packed stars and no trace of spiral arms.

Irregular dwarfs get less attention than spiral and elliptical galaxies, yet they are among the most common galaxies in the Universe. Astronomers suspect that some were once spirals or ellipticals that were later pulled out of shape by the gravity of nearby objects.

UGC 4459 holds young blue stars and older red ones, several billion in all. That sounds like a lot until you set it beside the Milky Way, home to 200 to 400 billion stars. Hubble observations show that small galaxies like this form stars at a very low rate, having turned only a little of their original gas into stars.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (2.75 x 1.99 arcminutes) and distance (11 million light years), the frame spans roughly 8,800 × 6,400 light-years. Its light set out about 11 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This image combines Hubble data from Wide Field Camera 3 and the Advanced Camera for Surveys, with filters from 275 to 814 nm spanning ultraviolet, visible and near-infrared light. The colours assigned to each filter are not published.
understand.eye: Ultraviolet and near-infrared light are invisible to the eye, and Hubble resolves individual stars in a galaxy that would look like a faint smudge otherwise.

explore: That makes them useful for studying conditions similar to the early Universe and the process of star formation itself. Ursa Major also contains the Pinwheel Galaxy (M101), the Owl Nebula (M97), and Messier 81 and Messier 82, along with other members of the M81 group.
alt: A diffuse, shapeless cloud of blue and red stars forming a dwarf galaxy.
